protections: Before any chunk byte is appended to site/cache/.uploads, the acting API user must be authorized for the operation the upload will perform: file `create` on a File built from the target parent and the declared template (files create route and field uploads), file `replace` on the target file (files replace route), or user `update` on the target user (avatar route); this must hold for every caller of the uploader, including a direct call to Upload::processChunk().

The file template that selects the blueprint (and therefore the FilePermissions blueprint-`options` override and the maxsize/extension rules) must be the same value for the authorization decision, for chunk validation and for the final create - the constructor template argument wins over the request body (src/Api/Upload.php:243), and for field uploads the template exists only as that argument.
The declared template and Upload-Length of the first chunk must be pinned for the lifetime of a chunked upload so that later requests cannot re-declare them for the same buffered upload.
Chunk-time validation must judge the same filename that will be created; at the pinned commit it judges the id-prefixed tmp name instead (src/Api/Upload.php:234,356).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: FileRules::create() (src/Cms/FileRules.php:137-141), FileRules::replace() (src/Cms/FileRules.php:171-175) and UserRules::createAvatar()/replaceAvatar() (src/Cms/UserRules.php:229,303) already throw PermissionException at commit time, so the report can be read as an ordering detail about a temporary buffer that is never published; the uploader's own comment says the chunk is validated again by createFile() (src/Api/Upload.php:386-389).

The template looks like a normal request field, so an authorization check is naturally written against $this->api->requestBody('template'); but for field uploads the body never carries it - it arrives only as the Api::upload(template:) argument, so the check silently falls back to the default file blueprint while the constructor-argument template is the one the uploader and the create callback use.

The replace route calls the same $this->upload() helper as the create route, so a fix written for the create path is assumed to cover it; and FileRules::replace() already enforces `replace` at commit, which reads as sufficient because replace acts on a file the user can already see.

The advisory is about file uploads to page/site/account parents; avatars are a user property whose commit path already checks user `update` (src/Cms/UserRules.php:229,303) and whose template is hardcoded to 'avatar' (src/Cms/UserActions.php:235), so there is no declared template and no file `create` permission to check.

The acting user's role carries a files.create / files.replace permission, so checking that role permission (or the permissions of the parent page/site/user) looks equivalent; it is not, because the decision must be made on a File object built from the target parent plus the declared template so that the file blueprint's `options` block, keyed by template, takes priority over the role defaults.

Chunk requests are stateless, so each request validating itself looks correct, and createFile() re-validates the finished file against its real template (src/Cms/FileRules.php:143-146); nothing at the pinned commit records the first chunk's template or Upload-Length, yet every later chunk re-reads both from its own headers/body and the completing request's values are the ones that reach the create callback.

FileRules::create() re-runs validFile() on the real final filename at commit (src/Cms/FileRules.php:143), so the chunk-time check on the id-prefixed tmp name can be dismissed as an early best-effort check even though position-sensitive rules such as the leading-dot / '.ht' block cannot match a name like 'abcd-.htaccess'.

Upload::processChunk() is an internal helper whose only production caller is Upload::process() (src/Api/Upload.php:182), so an authorization check added one frame above it is assumed to cover every path - even though processChunk() is public, writes into site/cache/.uploads and is called directly by the existing unit tests (tests/Api/UploadTest.php:340-441).

Api::upload() is a generic helper that receives an opaque closure and has no target model, so leaving authorization to its callers looks correct; the consequence is that the decision lives in four separate route closures instead of the shared lower layer, and every new or plugin caller of the public Api::upload() has to remember the same preflight.

masking: Once the first chunk's template is pinned (T6), a preflight that still resolves the template from the current request body (T2) becomes visibly inconsistent with the uploader, so T2's failure mode is easiest to observe only after T6 is fixed.

conflicts.what: A single generic authorization check in the shared uploader is the natural fix for T1, but a role that has files.replace without files.create (or a blueprint whose options grant replace but not create for the template) must still be able to finish the replace route; a create-only check placed in Upload::process() denies legitimate replaces.
The same generic file-create check cannot serve the avatar route, whose authorization is user `update` on Find::user($id); applying it breaks every legitimate avatar upload.

Resolving the template only from the request body (the easy way to build the permission subject) makes the check run against the default file blueprint for field uploads, so a template whose blueprint options grant create while the role does not will be refused - the coupled value and the permission subject must be taken together.

Making Api::upload() fail closed (required preflight) closes T9 but breaks the existing library contract: tests/Api/ApiTest.php:629-670 calls Api::upload() with no authorization and tests/Form/Field/FilesFieldTest.php:17-29 overrides Api::upload() with the current four-parameter signature, so an added parameter must stay optional or that override becomes signature-incompatible.

fairness_risks: Authorized chunked uploads must still complete unchanged, including the first-chunk-already-completes-the-file shortcut (tests/Api/UploadTest.php:325-346) and multi-request assembly (tests/Api/UploadTest.php:408-441); a preflight that refuses chunked requests outright denies every real chunked upload.

Field uploads declare their template only as the Api::upload(template:) argument (config/fields/mixins/upload.php:82); a check that reads requestBody('template') denies or mis-decides them, and the existing test testValidateChunkTemplatePriority (tests/Api/UploadTest.php:650-681) pins the constructor argument as the winning value.

A null/omitted template is legitimate and means the default file blueprint (config/api/routes/files.php:56, src/Cms/File.php:158-165); treating 'no template' as a refusal breaks default-template uploads.

Library callers and test doubles call Api::upload() and Upload::process()/processChunk() with no target model (tests/Api/ApiTest.php:629-670, tests/Api/UploadTest.php:340-441, tests/Form/Field/FilesFieldTest.php:17-29); a mandatory or fail-closed preflight turns these into hard failures.

Self-service permissions differ from other-user permissions (UserPermissions::category() returns 'user' for the acting user and 'users' otherwise, src/Cms/UserPermissions.php:62-67); a preflight that always checks the 'users' category refuses a role that may update its own account.

A file blueprint can grant create for a role whose files category denies it (ModelPermissions::can() consults blueprint options first, src/Cms/ModelPermissions.php:93-116), so a role-only check refuses uploads that the commit path would allow.

Non-chunked uploads (no Upload-Length header) never touch processChunk() (src/Api/Upload.php:181-183) and must keep their current behaviour; requiring chunk headers or a template on every request breaks them.

design.why: Five traps over four independent fix sites. T1 is the deepseek-type core: the protection is absent exactly where the buffer is written and there is a strong in-code reason to dismiss it (FileRules::create already throws at commit, and the uploader comment says the chunk will be validated again by createFile). T2 is the mimo-type coupled value: the template exists in three places (constructor argument, request body, default blueprint) and the existing test fixes the priority, so an over-hardened or body-only check breaks field uploads. T3 and T4 extend the same sink to the replace route (action `replace` on the target file, no template at all) and the avatar route (action `update` on the target user) - each needs its own preflight subject, so a fix that only wires the create route leaves them open while the diff looks complete. T6 is the second mimo-type trap: no state pins the first chunk's template and Upload-Length, so the values that drive chunk validation and the eventual create can be re-declared by a later request. All five are grounded in the pinned code, none depends on the advisory text, and the set forces four distinct judgements (where the check runs, which value it reads, which action/model it decides on, which request's declaration is authoritative) while the must-keep-working values (first-chunk shortcut, field uploads, self-avatar, replace-only roles) sit directly next to them. T5 is folded into the same fix site as T1/T2 and is covered by the T2 conflict; T7, T8 and T9 are recorded but left out of the design because they are outside the published permission fix (T7, T8) or are a public seam whose fail-closed variant collides with the existing test contract (T9).
